title: Penicillin Discovery Timeline
text:
In the late 1920s, microbiology laboratories often worked with open culture plates, and contamination was a routine problem rather than an unusual event. Researchers studying staphylococci frequently had to decide whether a spoiled sample was useless noise or a clue worth investigating.

Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital in London when he noticed that mold growing on a petri dish had killed nearby bacteria. Instead of throwing the dish away, he examined the pattern carefully and reported that the mold released a substance with strong antibacterial effects.

That first observation did not immediately create modern antibiotics, because purification and large-scale production took more time. Even so, Fleming's report became the starting point for later medical work that transformed infection treatment around the world.

title: Tokyo and Japan
text:
Japan has several globally important cities, each with a different historical and economic role. Osaka is known for commerce, Kyoto for imperial and cultural history, and Yokohama for trade and port activity.

The capital of Japan is Tokyo. It serves as the country's political center, hosts the national government, and functions as one of the largest metropolitan areas in the world.

Because Tokyo dominates finance, media, and transportation, many summaries about Japan mention it first. That prominence sometimes causes students to confuse the largest city, the capital city, and the wider metropolitan region, even though all three point to Tokyo in this case.

title: First iPhone Launch
text:
Before smartphones became mainstream, Apple was already known for combining hardware, software, and industrial design into tightly integrated consumer products. Rumors about a phone project circulated for months before the company made any formal announcement.

Apple announced the first iPhone in 2007 during a keynote presentation led by Steve Jobs. The launch introduced a touchscreen-centered interface and quickly became one of the most discussed product unveilings in consumer technology.

The commercial release happened later, which is why some people mix up the announcement year with the release date. For timeline questions, the key distinction is that the first announcement was in 2007.

title: Why Mars Is Called the Red Planet
text:
Planetary nicknames often come from visible surface features rather than formal scientific terminology. In school materials, these nicknames are useful because they make basic astronomy facts easier to remember.

Mars is known as the Red Planet because iron oxide on its surface gives it a reddish appearance when viewed from Earth. The color is visible enough that the nickname appears in both popular science writing and classroom explanations.

That label does not mean the entire planet is uniformly bright red, and it does not refer to temperature. It is simply a widely used description tied to surface chemistry and visual appearance.

title: Canada Capital and Major Cities
text:
Canada has several large and internationally recognizable cities, including Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, and Calgary. Because Toronto has the largest population and strongest global name recognition, many people incorrectly assume it is the political capital.

Ottawa is the capital of Canada. It was selected in the nineteenth century and today hosts the federal government, Parliament Hill, and many national institutions.

The distinction matters in question answering because population size and capital status are different attributes. Toronto is the largest city by population, while Ottawa is the capital city.

title: Python Language Origins
text:
Programming languages are often associated with a single creator even though communities later shape their development. In the case of Python, the early design reflected a preference for readability and practical scripting.

Python was created by Guido van Rossum. He began the project in the late 1980s, and the first public release appeared in 1991.

As Python grew, its ecosystem expanded far beyond one person's work. Even so, when a direct authorship question is asked, the correct answer remains Guido van Rossum.

title: The End of World War II
text:
The final phase of World War II unfolded differently across theaters, which is one reason students sometimes hesitate when asked for a single year. Major campaigns in Europe and Asia ended at different moments within the same broader period.

World War II ended in 1945. Germany surrendered in May 1945, and Japan surrendered later that year after the atomic bombings and Soviet entry into the Pacific war.

Because both major surrender events happened in the same calendar year, 1945 is the standard answer for general question answering prompts about when the war ended.

title: The Mona Lisa
text:
Famous paintings are often remembered through museums, styles, and stories of theft, but authorship remains the most common classroom fact. Renaissance works in particular are frequently used in basic art history quizzes.

The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo da Vinci. Today the painting is displayed in the Louvre Museum in Paris and is one of the most visited works of art in the world.

The painting's fame sometimes leads people to answer with the museum instead of the artist. For authorship questions, the correct response is Leonardo da Vinci.

title: The Periodic Table
text:
Chemists had proposed several ways to organize elements before the modern periodic table became widely accepted. The challenge was not only listing known substances, but arranging them so that patterns in their properties became visible.

Dmitri Mendeleev is often credited with creating the first widely recognized periodic table in 1869. His arrangement was notable because it grouped elements by recurring properties and even left space for elements that had not yet been discovered.

Later revisions improved accuracy as atomic theory advanced, but Mendeleev remains the central historical figure associated with the periodic table in standard educational contexts.

title: Mount Everest Overview
text:
The Himalayas contain several of the world's highest peaks, and mountaineering writing often discusses them together. That can make short factual questions sound deceptively simple because there are multiple ways to measure mountains.

Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level. It lies in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and China.

Some alternate rankings use base-to-summit measurements or volcanic base measurements, but when the question specifies above sea level, Mount Everest is the standard answer.

title: Water Boiling Point
text:
Temperature facts in science depend heavily on conditions, which is why careful explanations usually mention pressure. Without that context, a simple number can be misleading.

At standard atmospheric pressure, water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. This is the common classroom value used in introductory science and everyday reference material.

At higher altitudes the boiling point changes because pressure is lower, but if no special condition is stated, 100 degrees Celsius is the expected answer.

title: Speed of Light
text:
Physics constants are often introduced early in science education because they anchor many later ideas about relativity, optics, and electromagnetism. The exact unit matters, since textbooks may report the same constant in meters per second or kilometers per second.

The speed of light in vacuum is approximately 299,792 kilometers per second. In SI notation it is also commonly written as about 3.00 x 10^8 meters per second.

For quick factual retrieval, either form points to the same physical constant. The key idea is that the value refers to light traveling in vacuum, not through air or glass.

title: United Nations Founding
text:
The United Nations emerged from wartime planning and from dissatisfaction with earlier attempts at international cooperation. Leaders wanted a new institution that would be broader and more durable than the League of Nations.

The United Nations was founded in 1945 after World War II to promote international cooperation and reduce the likelihood of future global conflict. Its charter was signed in San Francisco and later entered into force that same year.

Because 1945 also marks the end of World War II, questions about the UN often appear next to broader postwar history topics. The founding year, however, remains straightforward: 1945.

title: The Great Wall of China
text:
Large historical structures are rarely the product of a single ruler or a single construction campaign. Instead, they evolve over long periods and across many political contexts.

The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications built across northern China over many dynasties. Different sections were constructed, repaired, and extended for different military and logistical purposes.

As a result, asking who built the Great Wall is usually less useful than asking what it is or why it exists. The most accurate summary is that it is a multi-dynasty defensive system.

title: The Amazon River
text:
Major rivers can be compared by length, discharge, drainage basin, or navigability, and different comparisons lead to different headlines. This is why educational summaries often focus on one or two uncontroversial facts.

The Amazon River is one of the longest rivers in the world and has the largest drainage basin. It flows across northern South America and plays a central role in regional ecology and transportation.

Because river rankings vary depending on method, the most stable statement is that the Amazon is among the world's longest rivers and has the largest drainage basin.

title: The Nobel Prizes
text:
Awards often outlive their founders, which can make the original historical connection less obvious to students. In many cases the founder's name remains visible while the legal and institutional background fades into the background.

Alfred Nobel established the Nobel Prizes in his will. The prizes were first awarded in 1901 and now recognize achievements in fields such as physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, peace, and economics.

Questions about the Nobel Prize may ask either who established it or when it was first awarded. Those answers are Alfred Nobel and 1901 respectively.

title: DNA and the Double Helix
text:
Biology textbooks often separate the definition of DNA from the history of discovering its structure. This can produce two different kinds of factual questions that sound similar but require different answers.

DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. The double helix structure was described by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953, drawing on several lines of prior experimental evidence.

When the question asks what DNA stands for, the expected response is the full term. When the question asks about the double helix, the historically associated names are Watson and Crick.

title: Origins of the Internet
text:
The modern internet did not appear in a single moment. It emerged from networking research, government-funded experiments, and later standardization work that connected previously separate systems.

The ARPANET project in the late 1960s is considered a key precursor to the modern internet. It demonstrated packet-switched networking and influenced later protocols that made large-scale internetworking possible.

Because the internet has many milestones, questions often accept broader answers than a simple inventor name. For introductory factual prompts, ARPANET is the most common reference point.

title: Basketball Invention
text:
Many modern sports evolved gradually, but basketball has an unusually well-documented origin story. That makes it a common example in classroom questions about invention and rules.

Basketball was invented by James Naismith in 1891 while he was teaching physical education in Springfield, Massachusetts. He designed the game as an indoor activity for winter training.

The original game looked different from modern professional basketball, but the inventor remains the same in every standard historical account: James Naismith.

title: Apollo 11 Moon Landing
text:
The space race produced many firsts, so lunar mission facts are often bundled together in a way that can confuse dates, crew names, and achievement types. Some questions ask for the mission, while others ask for the year or the astronaut.

Apollo 11 landed the first humans on the Moon in 1969. Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the lunar surface, followed by Buzz Aldrin.

If the prompt asks when the first Moon landing occurred, the expected answer is 1969. If it asks who first walked on the Moon, the answer is Neil Armstrong.
